1	# Stability and analysis options in Pynite
2	
3	This is a lightly formatted copy of the official Pynite manual at the
4	pre-fix source revision.  It is included as public scientific evidence, not as
5	an implementation hint.  Source: <https://github.com/JWock82/Pynite/blob/147c7aa24ec30b1c6a4d4820446915380752877b/docs/source/stability.rst>
6	and <https://github.com/JWock82/Pynite/blob/147c7aa24ec30b1c6a4d4820446915380752877b/docs/source/analysis.rst>.
7	
8	In a three-dimensional model, an object can translate in X, Y, or Z and rotate
9	about X, Y, or Z.  These three translations and three rotations are six
10	degrees of freedom, and all six must be stabilized for an object to be stable.
11	Rigid-body motion occurs when the entire structure can move as a unit because
12	supports are insufficient.  Localized nodal instabilities can remain after the
13	global structure is supported; hinged-ended members meeting at a node are one
14	example described by the manual.  Both situations appear as a singular,
15	unsolvable stiffness system.
16	
17	Pynite exposes a `check_stability=True` option on analysis methods to help
18	isolate these cases.  The manual also notes that the option costs extra
19	analysis time and is normally enabled while debugging a model.
20	
21	The analysis guide documents sparse and dense matrix solvers.  Sparse storage
22	keeps non-zero entries and is the default when SciPy is available; dense mode
23	stores all entries and can be useful for small models.  General analysis is
24	available through `FEModel3D.analyze()`, while `analyze_linear()` assembles a
25	linear model once and superposes load combinations.  These paths are both
26	used by the public workbench.
27	
28	Pynite's manual further distinguishes second-order P-Delta effects from the
29	first-order stability questions exercised here.  The workbench uses static
30	first-order cases so that the observations can be repeated without plotting,
31	network access, or external data.
32

34	see `source/LICENSE`.

10	def _model_from_case(case: dict, fixture: dict):

22	    )
23	    for name, x, y, z in case["nodes"]:
24	        model.add_node(name, x, y, z)
25	    for name, i, j in case["members"]:
26	        model.add_member(name, i, j, material["name"], section["name"])
27	
28	    for node in case.get("fixed_nodes", []):
29	        model.def_support(node, True, True, True, True, True, True)
30	    for node in case.get("pinned_nodes", []):
31	        # The end supports leave model-axis rotation free, as in a pin/roller
32	        # idealization; the member continuity supplies the remaining restraint.
33	        model.def_support(node, True, True, True, True, True, False)

35	    load = case["load"]

38	    else:

46	def _scalar(value) -> float:
47	    arr = np.asarray(value, dtype=float)
48	    return float(arr.reshape(-1)[0])
49

51	def _observe(model) -> dict[str, object]:
52	    displacements: list[float] = []
53	    reactions: list[float] = []
54	    for node in model.nodes.values():
55	        for field in (node.DX, node.DY, node.DZ, node.RX, node.RY, node.RZ):
56	            if "Combo 1" in field:
57	                displacements.append(_scalar(field["Combo 1"]))
58	        for field in (node.RxnFX, node.RxnFY, node.RxnFZ, node.RxnMX, node.RxnMY, node.RxnMZ):
59	            if "Combo 1" in field:
60	                reactions.append(_scalar(field["Combo 1"]))
61	    disp = np.asarray(displacements, dtype=float)
62	    rxn = np.asarray(reactions, dtype=float)
63	    max_disp = float(np.max(np.abs(disp))) if disp.size and np.isfinite(disp).all() else None
64	    reaction_l1 = float(np.sum(np.abs(rxn))) if rxn.size and np.isfinite(rxn).all() else None
65	    return {
66	        "finite_values": bool(np.isfinite(disp).all() and np.isfinite(rxn).all()),
67	        "max_abs_displacement": max_disp,
68	        "reaction_l1": reaction_l1,
69	        "displacement_count": int(disp.size),
70	    }

=========
Stability
=========

Perhaps the trickiest part of finite element modeling is making sure a model is stable. That may
sound trivial, but in finite element analysis it is nuanced. If you are getting "singularity"
errors in your model, it may not be as stable as you think it is. Remember that just because a
model is static does not mean it is stable.

Degrees of Freedom
==================
In 3 dimensions there are 6 "degrees of freedom" for motion to occur in. An object can translate
in either the X, Y or Z direction, and it can rotate about the X, Y or Z axis. These 3 translations
and 3 rotations together sum to 6 degrees of freedom. For an object to be stable, all 6 degrees
of freedom need to be stabilized

Instability Type 1: Rigid Body Motion
=====================================
Rigid body motion occurs when the entire structure can move as a unit in one of the 6 degrees of
freedom. This occurs when there is insufficient support for the structure. When rigid body motion
occurs, the stiffness matrix is "singular", and unsolvable. Adding supports can eliminate this type
of singularity.

Instability Type 2: Nodal Instability
=====================================
Once the global structure is stabilized, there may still be localized instabilities within it. Just
as all 6 degrees of freedom need to be constrained at the global level, so do instabilities at the
nodal (local) level need to be constrained. These types of instabilities also show up as
"singularities" in the stiffness matrix.

Consider a truss with multiple hinged-ended members framing into a node. What's to stop the node
from spinning if all the members it's attached to are hinged? The correct way to model this joint
would be to leave one of the member ends at the node unhinged. Rotations at the node would be then
be restrained by that member. It may be that there are no rotations at the node, but the degree of freedom
still needs to be tethered to a member (or a support) to make the node stable.

When selecting which member to tether the rotation to, consider what the connection looks like in
real life. If you were to apply a moment to the joint, where would it go? Unless you're dealing with
true pins, it will go somewhere. Even true pins are not frictionless (I've never seen them
perpetually rotating in the real world), and you may as well pick which member you want to assign
stray forces at that degree of freedom to.

Pynite can help you isolate these types of instabilities by passing ``check_stability=True`` to
any of the analysis methods (see below for an example). Note that this does slow down analysis, so
you usually only want to do this when you are debugging a model.

.. code-block:: python

    my_model.analyze(check_stability=True)

Instability Type 3: Second Order Effects
========================================
Once the Type 1 and Type 2 instabilities are rooted out of your model, there may be a third type of instability lurking quietly inside it. These types of instabilities can go unnoticed without careful attention to the analysis procedure.

Most material codes recognize that a first-order analysis is often not enough. As a structure deforms under load, the geometry changes, making the analysis results invalid. This requires us to reanalyze the structure under the new deformed geometry.

The P-:math:`\Delta` analysis feature is one tool Pynite provides to help check for this type of instability. P-:math:`\Delta` analysis is but one piece of the overall picture, which is usually defined by the material's building code. Additional considerations are usually necessary to capture this behavior, such as P-:math:`\delta` analysis, material stiffness reductions and notional loads. Note also that Pynite only performs P-:math:`\Delta` analysis for members. P-:math:`\Delta` effects are not considered for plates. See :doc:`PDelta` for more information.

Second order effects are usually only critical for models with slender members, or members with high axial loads in the presence of bending moments. If you don't have these types of features in your model, second order effects may be negligible. Consult your building code for specific criteria in making this determination. Either way, running a P-Delta analysis can help identify erorrs in the model you may have been unaware of. A model that cannot pass a P-Delta analysis is often something you don't really want to build.
==========
========
Analysis
========

`Pynite` offers several analysis options you can choose from. This section will help you identify the anlysis options you want to run.

Sparse vs. Dense Solvers
========================

Each of the analysis options in Pynite allows you to use either a sparse or dense matrix solver. The dense matrix solver stores all the values in the stiffness matrix, whereas the sparse solver only stores non-zero values. Both solvers provide correct solutions, but each will perform differently depending on your model.

The sparse solver is the default solver used by Pynite. It is well suited to large models. It uses less memory and solves large models faster. It solves small models slower, but usually the difference is not noticed because the models are small anyway. In order to use it you'll need to have ``Scipy`` installed.

You can switch to the dense solver by passing ``sparse=False`` to the analysis method you are using. ``Scipy`` does not need to be installed to use the dense solver. The dense solver is well suited to small models. If you need to repeatedly solve a small model, the dense solver can offer some performance advantages over the sparse solver.

General Analysis
================

Use the ``FEModel3D.analyze()`` method to run a general analysis. This analysis is iterative if there are tension-only or compression-only elements or supports in the model.

Linear Analysis
===============

Linear analysis can be performed by using the ``FEModel3D.analyze_linear()`` method. This method of analysis is very fast, but is limited to models without nonlinear features such as tension-only or compression-only elements and supports, or P-:math:`\Delta` effects. This method only needs to assemble the stiffness matrix once because it uses analytical superposition of forces to generate load combinations. Superposition requires a linear model.

P-:math:`\Delta` Analysis
=========================

P-:math:`\Delta` analysis is required by many building codes for frame structures. It covered in great detail here: :doc:`PDelta`

Other Useful Options
====================

You can pass a few other parameters to each analysis. To check statics use `check_statics=True` in the analysis command. To check stability use the `check_stability=True` option. Note that this option does slow down solution speed.
======
No external image or dataset asset is required for this deterministic, CPU-only
structural workbench.  The public method evidence is reproduced in `paper.md`
and the versioned documentation under `source/docs/source/`.

from scipy.sparse.linalg import splu, spsolve
from scipy.linalg import lu_factor
from Pynite import Analysis
from workflow.workbench import _model_from_case

def metrics(K11, label):
    K = np.asarray(K11.todense() if sps.issparse(K11) else K11, dtype=float)
    n = K.shape[0]
    d = np.diag(K).copy()
    out = {}
    out['n'] = n
    out['min_diag'] = d.min()
    w = np.linalg.eigvalsh(K)
    out['eig_ratio'] = w.min()/w.max()
    # Jacobi scaled
    s = 1/np.sqrt(np.where(d>0, d, 1.0))
    Kh = K * s[:,None] * s[None,:]
    wh = np.linalg.eigvalsh(Kh)
    out['scaled_eig_ratio'] = wh.min()/wh.max()
    # LU pivots dense
    lu, piv = lu_factor(Kh)
    u = np.abs(np.diag(lu))
    out['dense_pivot_ratio'] = u.min()/u.max()
    # SPLU pivots sparse
    slu = splu(sps.csc_matrix(Kh))
    us = np.abs(slu.U.diagonal())
    out['splu_pivot_ratio'] = us.min()/us.max()
    # natural-order, no partial pivoting (LDL-like)
    try:
        slu2 = splu(sps.csc_matrix(Kh), permc_spec='NATURAL', diag_pivot_thresh=0.0,
                    options=dict(SymmetricMode=True))
        us2 = np.abs(slu2.U.diagonal())
        out['ldl_pivot_min'] = us2.min()
        out['ldl_pivot_argmin'] = int(np.argmin(us2))
    except Exception as e:
        out['ldl'] = f'{type(e).__name__}: {e}'
    # Cholesky
    try:
        np.linalg.cholesky(Kh); out['chol'] = 'ok'
    except Exception as e:
        out['chol'] = type(e).__name__
    print(label, json.dumps(out, indent=1, default=str))

    Analysis._prepare_model(model)
    D1, D2i, D2 = Analysis._partition_D(model)
    Kd = model.Ke('Combo 1', False, False, False)
    K11 = Analysis._partition(model, Kd, D1, D2i)[0]
    metrics(K11, case['name'])

import sys, json, warnings, numpy as np
sys.path.insert(0, 'source'); sys.path.insert(0, '.')
import scipy.sparse as sps
from scipy.sparse.linalg import spsolve, splu
from scipy.linalg import lu_factor, lu_solve
from Pynite import Analysis
from workflow.workbench import _model_from_case

fixture = json.loads(open('fixtures/workbench.json').read())

def parts(case, sparse):
    model = _model_from_case(case, fixture)
    Analysis._prepare_model(model)
    D1i, D2i, D2 = Analysis._partition_D(model)
    K = model.Ke('Combo 1', False, False, sparse)
    if sparse: K = K.tocsr()
    K11, K12, K21, K22 = Analysis._partition(model, K, D1i, D2i)
    FER1, FER2 = Analysis._partition(model, model.FER('Combo 1'), D1i, D2i)
    P1, P2 = Analysis._partition(model, model.P('Combo 1'), D1i, D2i)
    D2 = np.array(D2).reshape(len(D2), 1)
    if sparse:
        b = np.subtract(np.subtract(P1, FER1), K12.tocsr() @ D2)
    else:
        b = np.subtract(np.subtract(P1, FER1), np.matmul(K12, D2))
    return model, K11, b

for case in fixture['cases']:
    for sparse in (True, False):
        model, K11, b = parts(case, sparse)
        print(case['name'], 'sparse' if sparse else 'dense', 'K11', type(K11), K11.shape, 'b', type(b), b.shape, b.dtype)
        with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as wl:
            warnings.simplefilter('always')
            if sparse:
                x = spsolve(K11, b)
                print("  spsolve out:", type(x), np.shape(x))
            else:
                x = np.linalg.solve(K11, b)
                print("  solve out:", type(x), np.shape(x))
            print("  warnings:", [str(w.category.__name__)+":"+str(w.message)[:60] for w in wl])
        x = np.asarray(x).reshape(-1)
        # compare factorization-based
        if sparse:
            lu = splu(sps.csc_matrix(K11)); x2 = lu.solve(np.asarray(b).reshape(-1))
        else:
            luf = lu_factor(np.asarray(K11)); x2 = lu_solve(luf, np.asarray(b).reshape(-1))
        print("  max|x|", np.max(np.abs(x)), " factorized max|x|", np.max(np.abs(x2)), " maxdiff", np.max(np.abs(x-x2)))
        # residual
        K11d = np.asarray(K11.todense() if sps.issparse(K11) else K11, float)
        r = K11d @ x - np.asarray(b).reshape(-1)
        print("  ||r||inf/||b||inf =", np.max(np.abs(r))/max(np.max(np.abs(b)),1e-300), " ||b||inf", np.max(np.abs(b)))

        # Add shear stiffness terms to the stiffness matrix
        ke += ((B1.T @ Hs @ B1)*det_J1 +
              (B2.T @ Hs @ B2)*det_J2 +
              (B3.T @ Hs @ B3)*det_J3 +
              (B4.T @ Hs @ B4)*det_J4)
        
        # Following Bathe's recommendation for the drilling degree of freedom
        # from Example 4.19 in "Finite Element Procedures, 2nd Ed.", calculate
        # the drilling stiffness as 1/1000 of the smallest diagonal term in
        # the element's stiffness matrix. This is not theoretically correct,
        # but it allows the model to solve without singularities, and should
        # have a minimal effect on the final solution. Bathe recommends 1/1000
        # as a value that is weak enough but not so small that it affect the
        # results. Bathe recommends looking at all the diagonals in the
        # combined bending plus membrane stiffness matrix. Some of those terms
        # relate to translational stiffness. It seems more rational to only
        # look at the terms relating to rotational stiffness. That will be
        # Pynite's approach.
        ke_rz = min(abs(ke[1, 1]), abs(ke[2, 2]), abs(ke[4, 4]), abs(ke[5, 5]),
                   abs(ke[7, 7]), abs(ke[8, 8]), abs(ke[10, 10]), abs(ke[11, 11])
                   )/1000
        
        # Initialize the expanded stiffness matrix to all zeros
        ke_exp = np.zeros((24, 24))

        # Step through each term in the unexpanded stiffness matrix
        # i = Unexpanded matrix row
        for i in range(12):

            # j = Unexpanded matrix column
            for j in range(12):
                
                # Find the corresponding term in the expanded stiffness
                # matrix

                # m = Expanded matrix row
                if i in [0, 3, 6, 9]:  # indices associated with deflection in z
                    m = 2*i + 2
                if i in [1, 4, 7, 10]:  # indices associated with rotation about x
                    m = 2*i + 1
                if i in [2, 5, 8, 11]:  # indices associated with rotation about y
                    m = 2*i

"""Small structural models used while developing/validating the stability repair.

Each builder returns (model, analysis_kwargs).  `stable` models must analyze and
produce finite results; `unstable` models must be rejected by the library.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import sys
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
if str(ROOT / 'source') not in sys.path:
    sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT / 'source'))

from Pynite import FEModel3D


def _mat_sec(m):
    m.add_material('steel', 29000, 11200, 0.3, 0.284)
    m.add_section('S', 10, 100, 150, 250)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- stable models
def portal_frame():
    m = FEModel3D(); _mat_sec(m)
    m.add_node('b1', 0, 0, 0); m.add_node('t1', 0, 144, 0)
    m.add_node('t2', 180, 144, 0); m.add_node('b2', 180, 0, 0)
    m.add_member('c1', 'b1', 't1', 'steel', 'S')
    m.add_member('c2', 'b2', 't2', 'steel', 'S')
    m.add_member('beam', 't1', 't2', 'steel', 'S')
    m.def_support('b1', True, True, True, True, True, True)
    m.def_support('b2', True, True, True, True, True, True)
    m.add_node_load('t1', 'FX', 10)
    return m


def cantilever():
    m = FEModel3D(); _mat_sec(m)
    m.add_node('N1', 0, 0, 0); m.add_node('N2', 120, 0, 0)
    m.add_member('M1', 'N1', 'N2', 'steel', 'S')
    m.def_support('N1', True, True, True, True, True, True)
    m.add_node_load('N2', 'FY', -5)
    return m


def simple_beam():
    m = FEModel3D(); _mat_sec(m)
    m.add_node('N1', 0, 0, 0); m.add_node('N2', 120, 0, 0); m.add_node('N3', 240, 0, 0)
    m.add_member('M1', 'N1', 'N2', 'steel', 'S')
    m.add_member('M2', 'N2', 'N3', 'steel', 'S')
    m.def_support('N1', True, True, True, True, True, False)
    m.def_support('N3', False, True, True, False, True, False)
    m.def_support('N2', False, False, True, False, True, False)
    m.add_member_dist_load('M1', 'Fy', -0.5, -0.5)
    m.add_member_dist_load('M2', 'Fy', -0.5, -0.5)
    return m


def beam_with_internal_hinge():
    """Two spans with an internal hinge over the middle support: stable."""
    m = FEModel3D(); _mat_sec(m)
    m.add_node('N1', 0, 0, 0); m.add_node('N2', 120, 0, 0); m.add_node('N3', 240, 0, 0)
    m.add_member('M1', 'N1', 'N2', 'steel', 'S')
    m.add_member('M2', 'N2', 'N3', 'steel', 'S')
    m.def_support('N1', True, True, True, True, True, False)
    m.def_support('N2', False, True, True, False, True, False)
    m.def_support('N3', False, True, True, False, True, False)
    m.def_releases('M2', Rzi=True)
    m.add_member_dist_load('M1', 'Fy', -0.5, -0.5)
    m.add_member_dist_load('M2', 'Fy', -0.5, -0.5)
    return m


def truss_with_tether():
    """Hinged (truss) members with one member tethering each node's rotations."""
    m = FEModel3D(); _mat_sec(m)
    m.add_node('N1', 0, 0, 0); m.add_node('N2', 120, 0, 0)
    m.add_node('N3', 240, 0, 0); m.add_node('N4', 120, 96, 0)
    m.add_member('bot1', 'N1', 'N2', 'steel', 'S')
    m.add_member('bot2', 'N2', 'N3', 'steel', 'S')
    m.add_member('diag1', 'N1', 'N4', 'steel', 'S')
    m.add_member('diag2', 'N4', 'N3', 'steel', 'S')
    m.add_member('vert', 'N2', 'N4', 'steel', 'S')
    for name in ('diag1', 'diag2', 'vert'):
        m.def_releases(name, Ryi=True, Rzi=True, Ryj=True, Rzj=True)
    m.def_support('N1', True, True, True, True, True, False)
    m.def_support('N3', False, True, True, False, True, False)
    m.def_support('N2', False, False, True, False, False, False)
    m.def_support('N4', False, False, True, False, False, False)
    m.add_node_load('N4', 'FY', -8)
    return m


def spring_supported_beam(k=1.0e3):
    m = FEModel3D(); _mat_sec(m)
    m.add_node('N1', 0, 0, 0); m.add_node('N2', 120, 0, 0); m.add_node('N3', 240, 0, 0)
    m.add_member('M1', 'N1', 'N2', 'steel', 'S')
    m.add_member('M2', 'N2', 'N3', 'steel', 'S')
    m.def_support('N1', True, True, True, True, True, False)
    m.def_support('N3', False, True, True, False, True, False)
    m.def_support_spring('N2', 'DY', k)
    m.def_support('N2', False, False, True, False, True, False)
    m.add_member_dist_load('M1', 'Fy', -0.5, -0.5)
    m.add_member_dist_load('M2', 'Fy', -0.5, -0.5)
    return m


def stiff_spring_beam():
    return spring_supported_beam(k=1.0e12)


def quad_plate():
    m = FEModel3D()

    m.add_rectangle_mesh('MSH', 12, 96, 96, 6, 'concrete', element_type='Quad')
    m.meshes['MSH'].generate()
    for node in m.nodes.values():
        if round(node.X, 6) in (0, 96) or round(node.Y, 6) in (0, 96):
            m.def_support(node.name, True, True, True, True, True, True)
    for quad in m.quads.values():
        m.add_quad_surface_pressure(quad.name, 0.1)
    return m


def plate_mesh():
    m = FEModel3D()

    m.add_rectangle_mesh('MSH', 12, 96, 96, 6, 'concrete', element_type='Rect')
    m.meshes['MSH'].generate()
    for node in m.nodes.values():
        if round(node.X, 6) in (0, 96) or round(node.Y, 6) in (0, 96):
            m.def_support(node.name, True, True, True, True, True, True)
    for plate in m.plates.values():
        m.add_plate_surface_pressure(plate.name, 0.1)
    return m


def thin_plate_mesh():
    m = FEModel3D()
    m.add_material('steel', 29000, 11200, 0.3, 0.284)
    m.add_rectangle_mesh('MSH', 6, 48, 48, 0.05, 'steel', element_type='Quad')
    m.meshes['MSH'].generate()
    for node in m.nodes.values():
        if round(node.X, 6) in (0, 48) or round(node.Y, 6) in (0, 48):
            m.def_support(node.name, True, True, True, True, True, True)
    for quad in m.quads.values():
        m.add_quad_surface_pressure(quad.name, 0.01)
    return m


def slender_frame():
    """Mixed axial/flexural stiffness contrast (very slender members)."""
    m = FEModel3D()
    m.add_material('steel', 29000, 11200, 0.3, 0.284)
    m.add_section('slender', 1.0, 0.02, 0.02, 0.03)
    m.add_node('b1', 0, 0, 0); m.add_node('t1', 0, 600, 0)
    m.add_node('t2', 400, 600, 0); m.add_node('b2', 400, 0, 0)
    m.add_member('c1', 'b1', 't1', 'steel', 'slender')
    m.add_member('c2', 'b2', 't2', 'steel', 'slender')
    m.add_member('bm', 't1', 't2', 'steel', 'slender')
    m.def_support('b1', True, True, True, True, True, True)
    m.def_support('b2', True, True, True, True, True, True)
    m.add_node_load('t1', 'FX', 0.05)
    return m


def enforced_displacement():
    m = FEModel3D(); _mat_sec(m)
    m.add_node('N1', 0, 0, 0); m.add_node('N2', 120, 0, 0)
    m.add_member('M1', 'N1', 'N2', 'steel', 'S')
    m.def_support('N1', True, True, True, True, True, True)
    m.def_support('N2', False, True, True, False, False, False)
    m.def_node_disp('N2', 'DY', -0.5)
    return m


def tension_only_brace():
    m = FEModel3D(); _mat_sec(m)
    m.add_node('b1', 0, 0, 0); m.add_node('t1', 0, 144, 0)
    m.add_node('t2', 180, 144, 0); m.add_node('b2', 180, 0, 0)
    m.add_member('c1', 'b1', 't1', 'steel', 'S')
    m.add_member('c2', 'b2', 't2', 'steel', 'S')
    m.add_member('beam', 't1', 't2', 'steel', 'S')

    m.def_support('b2', True, True, True, True, True, True)
    m.add_node_load('t1', 'FX', 10)

def pdelta_frame():
    m = FEModel3D(); _mat_sec(m)
    m.add_node('b1', 0, 0, 0); m.add_node('t1', 0, 144, 0)
    m.add_member('c1', 'b1', 't1', 'steel', 'S')
    m.def_support('b1', True, True, True, True, True, True)
    m.def_support('t1', False, False, True, False, True, True)
    m.add_node_load('t1', 'FY', -50)
    m.add_node_load('t1', 'FX', 2)

STABLE = {

def plate_mesh(mesh_size, size=240, full_support=True):
    m = FEModel3D()
    m.add_material('concrete', 3824, 1593, 0.17, 0.150/12**3)
    m.add_rectangle_mesh('MSH', mesh_size, size, size, 8, 'concrete', element_type='Quad')
    m.meshes['MSH'].generate()
    nodes = list(m.nodes.values())
    if full_support:

    else:

    for q in m.quads.values():
        m.add_quad_surface_pressure(q.name, 0.05)
    return m

#%%
# The relative size a pivot of the equilibrated stiffness matrix has to fall below before
# the matrix is considered singular. See `_singularity_tolerance` below.
SINGULARITY_FLOOR = 100

# The largest equilibrium error a set of calculated displacements may have, relative to the
# loads that were applied to the structure, before the solution is rejected. See
# `_validate_displacements` below.
EQUILIBRIUM_RTOL = 1e-6

# Machine precision of the floating point numbers the stiffness matrix is assembled with
EPS = float(np.finfo(float).eps)


def _singularity_tolerance(size: int) -> float:
    """Returns the relative pivot size below which a stiffness matrix is considered singular.

    An unstable structure has a singular stiffness matrix, and a singular matrix cannot be
    factored. In exact arithmetic the solvers would simply fail on it, but the assembled
    matrix always carries round-off from adding up the element stiffness terms, so the
    matrix that actually reaches the solver is usually just barely non-singular. The
    solvers happily factor it and return displacements that are not a solution of anything.
    Singularity therefore has to be judged the same way rank is judged everywhere else in
    numerical linear algebra: relative to the round-off in the matrix.

    The tolerance returned is the matrix size times the machine precision, which is the
    standard numerical rank tolerance (it is the same tolerance `numpy.linalg.matrix_rank`
    uses by default), with a floor for small matrices so that the check is never tighter
    than the round-off generated while assembling and equilibrating the matrix.

    :param size: The number of degrees of freedom being solved for.
    :type size: int
    :return: The smallest pivot ratio a stable stiffness matrix may have.
    :rtype: float
    """

    return max(size, SINGULARITY_FLOOR)*EPS


def _dof_direction(dof: int) -> str:
    """Returns a description of the direction a global degree of freedom acts in.

    :param dof: The index of the degree of freedom in the global stiffness matrix.
    :type dof: int
    :return: A description of the degree of freedom's direction.
    :rtype: str
    """

    if dof % 6 == 0:
        return 'for translation in the global X direction.'
    elif dof % 6 == 1:
        return 'for translation in the global Y direction.'
    elif dof % 6 == 2:
        return 'for translation in the global Z direction.'
    elif dof % 6 == 3:
        return 'for rotation about the global X axis.'
    elif dof % 6 == 4:
        return 'for rotation about the global Y axis.'
    else:
        return 'for rotation about the global Z axis.'


def _dof_name(model: FEModel3D, dof: int) -> str:
    """Returns a description of a global degree of freedom's node and direction.

    :param model: The model the degree of freedom belongs to.
    :type model: FEModel3D
    :param dof: The index of the degree of freedom in the global stiffness matrix.
    :type dof: int
    :return: A description of the degree of freedom.
    :rtype: str
    """

    # Find the node this degree of freedom belongs to
    node = None
    for candidate in model.nodes.values():
        if candidate.ID == dof//6:
            node = candidate
            break

    name = node.name if node is not None else 'with ID ' + str(dof//6)

    return 'node ' + name + ' ' + _dof_direction(dof)


def _row_maximums(K, sparse: bool) -> NDArray[float64]:
    """Returns the largest absolute value in each row of a stiffness matrix.

    :param K: A stiffness matrix.
    :type K: ndarray | scipy sparse matrix
    :param sparse: Indicates whether `K` is a `scipy` sparse matrix.
    :type sparse: bool
    :return: The largest absolute value in each row of `K`.
    :rtype: NDArray[float64]
    """

    if K.shape[0] == 0:
        return zeros(0)

    if sparse:
        row_max = abs(K.tocsr()).max(axis=1)
        if hasattr(row_max, 'toarray'):
            row_max = row_max.toarray()
    else:
        row_max = np.max(np.abs(np.asarray(K, dtype=float)), axis=1)

    return np.asarray(row_max, dtype=float).reshape(-1)


class _Equilibrated():
    """A factored copy of a stiffness matrix that can be tested for singularity.

    The rows and columns of the matrix are scaled by the square root of the largest
    stiffness term in each row before the matrix is factored. That scaling is symmetric, so
    it cannot turn a singular matrix into a non-singular one, but it does put every
    diagonal term of the scaled matrix on the order of 1. The pivots of the factored matrix
    can then be compared to each other no matter what units the model was built in, or how
    the axial, flexural, torsional, plate and spring stiffness terms in it are mixed
    together.

    :param K: The partitioned stiffness matrix for the degrees of freedom being solved for.
    :type K: ndarray | scipy sparse matrix
    :param sparse: Indicates whether `K` is a `scipy` sparse matrix.
    :type sparse: bool
    """

    def __init__(self, K, sparse: bool) -> None:

        self.sparse = bool(sparse)
        self.size = int(K.shape[0])

        # Get the reference stiffness for each degree of freedom. A row of zeros means
        # nothing in the model provides any stiffness for that degree of freedom at all.
        row_max = _row_maximums(K, self.sparse)
        self.scale = np.ones(self.size)
        stiff = row_max > 0
        self.scale[stiff] = 1/np.sqrt(row_max[stiff])

        # Factor the equilibrated matrix. `pivot_ratio` is the smallest pivot of the
        # factorization relative to the largest one, which measures how much stiffness the
        # structure has left in its softest direction. A ratio at the level of machine
        # precision means it has none left, in other words that it is unstable.
        self._solve = None
        self.pivot_ratio = 1.0

        if self.size > 0:
            pivots, self._solve = _factor_equilibrated(K, self.scale, self.sparse)

            if pivots is None or pivots.size != self.size or not np.isfinite(pivots).all():
                # The matrix could not be factored at all, which means it is exactly singular
                self.pivot_ratio = 0.0
            else:
                largest = float(np.max(pivots))
                self.pivot_ratio = float(np.min(pivots))/largest if largest > 0 else 0.0

    @property
    def is_singular(self) -> bool:
        """Indicates whether the stiffness matrix is singular to within round-off.

        :return: `True` if the matrix is singular, which means the structure is unstable.
        :rtype: bool
        """

        return self.pivot_ratio <= _singularity_tolerance(self.size)

    def unstable_shape(self) -> Optional[NDArray[float64]]:
        """Returns an estimate of the displaced shape the structure has no stiffness in.

        The estimate comes from inverse iteration: solving a nearly singular system
        magnifies whatever part of the right hand side lines up with the softest direction
        of the matrix, so after a couple of solutions the result is dominated by that
        direction. It is only used to tell the user which degrees of freedom take part in
        the instability, so a rough estimate is all that is needed.

        :return: The unstable shape, normalized so its largest component is 1, or `None` if
                 it could not be estimated.
        :rtype: NDArray[float64] | None
        """

        if self._solve is None:
            return None

        # Start from a fixed pseudo-random vector so the diagnostics are repeatable
        shape = None
        vector = np.random.default_rng(0).standard_normal(self.size)

        for _ in range(2):

            try:
                with catch_warnings():
                    simplefilter('ignore')
                    with np.errstate(all='ignore'):
                        candidate = np.asarray(self._solve(vector), dtype=float).reshape(-1)
            except Exception:
                break

            largest = float(np.max(np.abs(candidate))) if candidate.size > 0 else 0.0

            if not np.isfinite(largest) or largest == 0:
                break

            vector = candidate/largest
            shape = vector

        if shape is None:
            return None

        # Undo the equilibration so the shape is expressed in the model's degrees of freedom
        shape = self.scale*shape
        largest = float(np.max(np.abs(shape)))

        if not np.isfinite(largest) or largest == 0:
            return None

        return shape/largest


def _factor_equilibrated(K, scale: NDArray[float64], sparse: bool) -> Tuple[Optional[NDArray[float64]], Optional[Callable]]:
    """Factors a symmetrically scaled stiffness matrix.

    :param K: The stiffness matrix to factor.
    :type K: ndarray | scipy sparse matrix
    :param scale: The scale factor for each row/column of `K`.
    :type scale: NDArray[float64]
    :param sparse: Indicates whether `K` is a `scipy` sparse matrix.
    :type sparse: bool
    :return: The magnitudes of the factorization's pivots, and a function that solves the
             scaled system of equations. Both are `None` if the matrix could not be
             factored, which happens when it is exactly singular.
    :rtype: tuple
    """

    if sparse:

        from scipy.sparse import diags
        from scipy.sparse.linalg import splu

        S = diags(scale)
        K_scaled = (S @ K.tocsr() @ S).tocsc()

        try:
            with catch_warnings():
                simplefilter('ignore')
                factorization = splu(K_scaled)
        except Exception:
            # `SuperLU` refuses to factor a matrix with an exactly zero pivot in it
            return None, None

        return np.abs(factorization.U.diagonal()), factorization.solve

    K_scaled = np.asarray(K, dtype=float)*scale.reshape(-1, 1)*scale.reshape(1, -1)

    try:
        from scipy.linalg import lu_factor, lu_solve
    except ImportError:
        # The dense solver does not require `scipy`. Without it the singular values of the
        # scaled matrix are used to measure its rank instead of the pivots of an `LU`
        # factorization.
        try:
            with catch_warnings():
                simplefilter('ignore')
                singular_values = np.linalg.svd(K_scaled, compute_uv=False)
        except Exception:
            return None, None

        return singular_values, (lambda b: solve(K_scaled, b))

    try:
        with catch_warnings():
            simplefilter('ignore')
            factorization = lu_factor(K_scaled)
    except Exception:
        return None, None

    return np.abs(np.diag(factorization[0])), (lambda b: lu_solve(factorization, b))


def _report_instability(model: FEModel3D, D1_indices: List[int], equilibrated: _Equilibrated) -> None:
    """Prints a description of a singular stiffness matrix to the console.

    :param model: The model the stiffness matrix was assembled from.
    :type model: FEModel3D
    :param D1_indices: The indices of the degrees of freedom being solved for.
    :type D1_indices: List[int]
    :param equilibrated: The factored stiffness matrix that was found to be singular.
    :type equilibrated: _Equilibrated
    """

    print('* Instability detected: the stiffness matrix is singular. The structure can '
          + 'displace without resistance, which means it is either not fully supported '
          + '(rigid body motion) or it contains a mechanism.')

    # Report the degrees of freedom that participate the most in the unstable displaced
    # shape. Those are the ones the user needs to look at.
    shape = equilibrated.unstable_shape()

    if shape is None:
        return

    for index in np.argsort(-np.abs(shape)):

        # Only report degrees of freedom that displace by a meaningful fraction of the
        # largest displacement in the unstable shape
        if abs(shape[index]) < 0.01:
            break

        print('* Instability detected: ' + _dof_name(model, D1_indices[index])
              + ' The structure can displace at this degree of freedom without resistance.')


def _check_stability(model: FEModel3D, K: NDArray[float64]) -> None:
    """
    Identifies nodal instabilities in a model's stiffness matrix.

    Both types of first order instability described in Pynite's documentation leave the
    stiffness matrix singular:

    * Rigid body motion, where the structure, or a part of it, can move as a unit because
      it is not supported in one of its degrees of freedom.
    * Nodal instability, where a degree of freedom at a node has nothing to restrain it.
      Members framing into a node with all of their ends released are the classic example.

    Degrees of freedom that have no stiffness at all are reported one by one, since those
    are the easiest for the user to correct. Instabilities that involve several degrees of
    freedom at once, such as rigid body motion or a mechanism formed by member end
    releases, do not leave a zero on the diagonal of the stiffness matrix, so they are
    found by testing the partitioned matrix the solvers have to invert for rank deficiency.

    :param model: The model to check for instabilities.
    :type model: FEModel3D
    :param K: The model's global stiffness matrix, including its supported degrees of freedom.
    :type K: ndarray | scipy sparse matrix
    :raises Exception: Occurs when the model is unstable.
    """

    # Determine whether a sparse or a dense stiffness matrix is being checked
    sparse = hasattr(K, 'tocsr')

    # Get the degrees of freedom the solvers will be solving for. Degrees of freedom with a
    # support or an enforced displacement are known, so they cannot be unstable.
    D1_indices, D2_indices, D2 = _partition_D(model)

    # Initialize the `unstable` flag to `False`
    unstable = False

    # Get the diagonal of the stiffness matrix, and the largest stiffness term in each of
    # its rows for reference
    diagonal = np.asarray(K.diagonal() if sparse else np.diag(K), dtype=float).reshape(-1)
    row_max = _row_maximums(K, sparse)

    # Step through each degree of freedom that is being solved for
    for dof in D1_indices:

        # Check if the degree of freedom on this diagonal is unstable. A zero on the
        # diagonal means nothing in the model - no element and no support - restrains this
        # degree of freedom.
        if diagonal[dof] <= _singularity_tolerance(len(D1_indices))*row_max[dof]:

            # Flag the model as unstable
            unstable = True

            # Print a message to the console
            print('* Nodal instability detected: ' + _dof_name(model, dof).replace('node ', 'node ', 1).replace(' for', ' is unstable for', 1))

    # A model can have stiffness at every one of its degrees of freedom and still be
    # unstable. Test the partitioned stiffness matrix, which is the matrix that actually
    # gets solved, for the loss of rank that rigid body motion and mechanisms cause.
    if unstable is False and len(D1_indices) > 0:

        K11 = _partition(model, K, D1_indices, D2_indices)[0]
        equilibrated = _Equilibrated(K11, sparse)

        if equilibrated.is_singular:
            unstable = True
            _report_instability(model, D1_indices, equilibrated)

    if unstable:
        raise Exception('Unstable node(s). The stiffness matrix is singular, which means the structure is unstable. See console output for details.')

    return


def _solve_displacements(model: FEModel3D, K11, P: NDArray[float64], D1_indices: List[int], sparse: bool = True, check_stability: bool = False, log: bool = False) -> NDArray[float64]:
    """Solves `[K11]{D1} = {P}` for the unknown displacements of a load combination or load step.

    The solution is validated before it is returned. A direct solver is not required to
    fail on a singular stiffness matrix: round-off in the assembled matrix normally leaves
    it just barely factorable, in which case the solver returns displacements that do not
    satisfy the equations that were handed to it. Those displacements are usually
    non-finite or absurdly large, and they depend on which solver was used, so they cannot
    be reported as the structure's response. Checking them against the equations they came
    from catches this for any solver, and it costs one matrix-vector product.

    :param model: The model being analyzed.
    :type model: FEModel3D
    :param K11: The partitioned stiffness matrix for the degrees of freedom being solved for.
    :type K11: ndarray | scipy sparse matrix
    :param P: The load vector for the degrees of freedom being solved for.
    :type P: NDArray[float64]
    :param D1_indices: The indices of the degrees of freedom being solved for.
    :type D1_indices: List[int]
    :param sparse: Indicates whether the sparse solver should be used. Default is `True`.
    :type sparse: bool
    :param check_stability: Indicates whether `K11` should be checked for instabilities
                            before it is solved. Default is `False`. This is only needed
                            for matrices that `FEModel3D.Ke` has not already checked, such
                            as ones that include geometric or plastic stiffness terms.
    :type check_stability: bool
    :param log: Indicates whether analysis logs should be printed. Default is `False`.
    :type log: bool
    :raises Exception: Occurs when the stiffness matrix is singular, which means the
                       structure is unstable.
    :return: The calculated displacements.
    :rtype: NDArray[float64]
    """

    # Check the matrix that is about to be solved for instabilities if requested
    if check_stability:

        if log:
            print('- Checking the stiffness matrix for instabilities')

        equilibrated = _Equilibrated(K11, sparse)

        if equilibrated.is_singular:
            _report_instability(model, D1_indices, equilibrated)
            raise Exception('The stiffness matrix is singular, which means the structure is unstable.')

    # Solve the system of equations for the unknown displacements
    if sparse == True:

        from scipy.sparse.linalg import spsolve

        # The partitioned stiffness matrix originates as `coo` and is converted to `csr`
        # format for mathematical operations.
        with catch_warnings():
            simplefilter('ignore')
            with np.errstate(all='ignore'):
                D1 = spsolve(K11.tocsr(), P)

        D1 = np.asarray(D1, dtype=float).reshape(-1, 1)

    else:

        with catch_warnings():
            simplefilter('ignore')
            with np.errstate(all='ignore'):
                D1 = solve(K11, P)

    # Make sure the displacements the solver returned really are a solution of the
    # equations that were solved
    _validate_displacements(model, K11, D1, P, D1_indices, sparse)

    return D1


def _validate_displacements(model: FEModel3D, K11, D1: NDArray[float64], P: NDArray[float64], D1_indices: List[int], sparse: bool = True) -> None:
    """Verifies that a set of calculated displacements is a valid solution of `[K11]{D1} = {P}`.

    :param model: The model being analyzed.
    :type model: FEModel3D
    :param K11: The partitioned stiffness matrix that was solved.
    :type K11: ndarray | scipy sparse matrix
    :param D1: The calculated displacements.
    :type D1: NDArray[float64]
    :param P: The load vector that was solved for.
    :type P: NDArray[float64]
    :param D1_indices: The indices of the degrees of freedom being solved for.
    :type D1_indices: List[int]
    :param sparse: Indicates whether `K11` is a `scipy` sparse matrix. Default is `True`.
    :type sparse: bool
    :raises Exception: Occurs when the displacements are not a valid solution, which means
                       the stiffness matrix is singular and the structure is unstable.
    """

    D1 = np.asarray(D1, dtype=float).reshape(-1, 1)
    P = np.asarray(P, dtype=float).reshape(-1, 1)

    if D1.size == 0:
        return

    # Displacements that are not finite are never a valid solution
    if not np.isfinite(D1).all():
        print('* Instability detected: the solver returned displacements that are not finite. '
              + 'The stiffness matrix is singular, which means the structure is unstable.')
        raise Exception('The stiffness matrix is singular, which means the structure is unstable.')

    # Calculate how far the displacements are from satisfying the equations of equilibrium
    # that were solved. The error is measured against the loads that were applied to the
    # structure, since a set of displacements that does not carry the applied loads is not
    # a static solution of the model.
    with catch_warnings():
        simplefilter('ignore')
        with np.errstate(all='ignore'):
            residual = np.asarray(K11 @ D1, dtype=float).reshape(-1, 1) - P

    error = float(nanmax(np.abs(residual))) if residual.size > 0 else 0.0
    applied = float(nanmax(np.abs(P))) if P.size > 0 else 0.0

    if not np.isfinite(error) or error > EQUILIBRIUM_RTOL*applied:

        # Report the degree of freedom that is furthest out of equilibrium
        dof = D1_indices[int(np.argmax(np.abs(np.nan_to_num(residual))))]

        print('* Instability detected: the calculated displacements do not satisfy equilibrium at '
              + _dof_name(model, dof) + ' The stiffness matrix is singular, which means the '
              + 'structure is unstable.')

        raise Exception('The stiffness matrix is singular, which means the structure is unstable.')

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The singularity criterion itself
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
def test_singularity_criterion_is_scale_invariant():
    """The criterion depends on the shape of the matrix, not on the units of the model."""

    # A stiffness matrix for two degrees of freedom connected by a spring, plus a support
    K = np.array([[2.0, -1.0], [-1.0, 1.0]])
    singular = np.array([[1.0, -1.0], [-1.0, 1.0]])

    for factor in (1e-12, 1.0, 1e12):
        assert not Analysis._Equilibrated(factor*K, False).is_singular
        assert Analysis._Equilibrated(factor*singular, False).is_singular

    # Mixed units: one degree of freedom in inches, the other in miles
    scale = np.diag([1.0, 63360.0])
    assert not Analysis._Equilibrated(scale @ K @ scale, False).is_singular
    assert Analysis._Equilibrated(scale @ singular @ scale, False).is_singular


def test_singularity_criterion_flags_missing_stiffness():
    """A degree of freedom with no stiffness is a singular matrix, at any size."""

    for size in (2, 10, 60):
        K = np.eye(size)
        assert not Analysis._Equilibrated(K, False).is_singular
        K[size//2, size//2] = 0.0
        assert Analysis._Equilibrated(K, False).is_singular

    """An ill-conditioned but non-singular matrix is not called singular."""

        assert not Analysis._Equilibrated(K, False).is_singular

133	    matrix always carries round-off from adding up the element stiffness terms, so the
134	    matrix that actually reaches the solver is usually just barely non-singular. The

def _report_instability(model: FEModel3D, D1_indices: List[int], equilibrated: _Equilibrated) -> None:
    """Prints a description of a singular stiffness matrix to the console.

    :param model: The model the stiffness matrix was assembled from.
    :type model: FEModel3D
    :param D1_indices: The indices of the degrees of freedom being solved for.
    :type D1_indices: List[int]
    :param equilibrated: The factored stiffness matrix that was found to be singular.
    :type equilibrated: _Equilibrated
    """

    print('* Instability detected: the stiffness matrix is singular. The structure can '
          + 'displace without resistance, which means it is either not fully supported '
          + '(rigid body motion) or it contains a mechanism.')

    # Report the degrees of freedom that participate the most in the unstable displaced
    # shape. Those are the ones the user needs to look at.
    shape = equilibrated.unstable_shape()

    if shape is None:
        return

    # Only report degrees of freedom that displace by a meaningful fraction of the largest
    # displacement in the unstable shape
    involved = [index for index in np.argsort(-np.abs(shape)) if abs(shape[index]) >= 0.01]

    for index in involved[0:REPORT_LIMIT]:
        print('* Instability detected: ' + _dof_name(model, D1_indices[index])
              + ' The structure can displace at this degree of freedom without resistance.')

Pynite can help you isolate these types of instabilities by passing ``check_stability=True`` to
any of the analysis methods (see below for an example). Note that this does slow down analysis, so
you usually only want to do this when you are debugging a model.

.. code-block:: python

    my_model.analyze(check_stability=True)

How Pynite Detects a Singular Stiffness Matrix
==============================================
Both of the instability types above leave the stiffness matrix singular, and a singular matrix has
no unique solution. It is worth knowing how Pynite reaches that conclusion, because a stiffness
matrix is never exactly singular once it has been assembled in floating point arithmetic: round-off
almost always leaves it just barely invertible, and a direct solver will happily factor it and hand
back displacements that are not a solution of anything. Those displacements are typically
non-finite, absurdly large, or different from one solver to the next.

Pynite therefore does two things instead of relying on the solver to fail:

* With ``check_stability=True`` it tests the stiffness matrix for numerical rank deficiency. Every
  degree of freedom is scaled by the largest stiffness term in its row, which makes the test
  independent of the units of your model, and the pivots of the factored matrix are then compared
  to each other. A degree of freedom left with no stiffness relative to the rest of the model means
  the structure can displace without resistance, and the degrees of freedom involved are reported to
  the console. This catches instabilities that no single term of the matrix reveals on its own, such
  as rigid body motion of the whole structure or a mechanism formed by member end releases.

* Whether or not you ask for the stability check, every set of displacements Pynite solves for is
  checked against the equations of equilibrium it came from before it is reported. Displacements
  that are not finite, or that do not carry the loads that were applied to the structure, are
  rejected with a singular stiffness matrix error rather than being reported as your structure's
  response.

Either way an unstable model raises an exception. If you get one, the console output names the nodes
and directions to look at.

"""Compares the repaired library against the historical snapshot it was made from.

Every model in `models.py` is analyzed twice, once with the library as it is committed in
`HEAD` and once with the working copy, and the results are compared. Supported structures
have to give exactly the same numbers as before; unsupported ones have to stop being
reported.

Usage::

    python devtests/compare_with_baseline.py
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import json
import os
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]

WORKER = '''
import io, json, sys, contextlib
import numpy as np
import models

results = {}
for group, builders in (('stable', models.STABLE), ('unstable', models.UNSTABLE)):
    for name in sorted(builders):
        for method in ('analyze', 'analyze_linear'):
            for sparse in (True, False):
                for check_stability in (True, False):
                    key = '|'.join((group, name, method, str(sparse), str(check_stability)))
                    model = builders[name]()
                    try:
                        with contextlib.redirect_stdout(io.StringIO()):
                            getattr(model, method)(check_stability=check_stability, sparse=sparse)
                        results[key] = {combo: np.asarray(D).reshape(-1).tolist()
                                        for combo, D in model._D.items()}
                    except Exception as exception:
                        results[key] = type(exception).__name__

json.dump(results, open(sys.argv[1], 'w'))
'''


def run(source: Path, output: Path) -> dict:
    """Analyzes every model with the copy of the library in `source`."""

    environment = dict(os.environ, PYNITE_SOURCE=str(source), PYTHONPATH=str(ROOT / 'devtests'),
                       PYTHONWARNINGS='ignore')
    subprocess.run([sys.executable, '-c', WORKER, str(output)], env=environment, check=True,
                   cwd=str(ROOT))

    return json.loads(output.read_text())


def main() -> int:

    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as directory:

        directory = Path(directory)

        # Materialize the library as it was before the repair
        baseline = directory / 'baseline'
        baseline.mkdir()
        archive = subprocess.run(['git', 'archive', 'HEAD', 'source'], cwd=str(ROOT),
                                 capture_output=True, check=True).stdout
        subprocess.run(['tar', '-x', '-C', str(baseline)], input=archive, check=True)

        before = run(baseline / 'source', directory / 'before.json')
        after = run(ROOT / 'source', directory / 'after.json')

    changed, broken = [], []

    for key in sorted(before):

        if before[key] == after[key]:
            continue

        if key.startswith('stable'):
            broken.append(key)
        else:
            changed.append(key)

    print(f'{len(before)} analyses compared\n')

    print('Unsupported structures that are no longer reported as a static result:')
    for key in changed:
        was = before[key] if isinstance(before[key], str) else \
            'max|D| = ' + f'{max(max(map(abs, D)) for D in before[key].values()):.6g}'
        now = after[key] if isinstance(after[key], str) else \
            'max|D| = ' + f'{max(max(map(abs, D)) for D in after[key].values()):.6g}'
        print(f'  {key:62s} {was:>22s} -> {now}')

    print(f'\nSupported structures whose results changed: {len(broken)}')
    for key in broken:
        print(f'  {key}')

    return 1 if broken else 0


if __name__ == '__main__':
    raise SystemExit(main())

The repair is complete and verified end to end.

## What was wrong

`frame_b` in the workbench is a **genuine one-degree-of-freedom mechanism**: an internal moment release (`def_releases('m2', Rzi=True)`) in a simply supported beam. Its free stiffness partition is singular, so there is no unique static answer — but neither `spsolve` nor `numpy.linalg.solve` fails on it, because assembly round-off leaves the matrix barely factorable. The historical `_check_stability` only looked for *exactly zero* diagonal terms (`isclose(K[i,i], 0)`), which a mechanism never produces, so the snapshot reported `max|D| ≈ 2.9e17` (sparse) vs `1.9e17` (dense) as if it were a result: non-finite/implausible and solver-dependent, exactly as `paper.md` describes for Type 1/Type 2 instabilities.

## The fix (two layers, both unit-independent and model-agnostic)

1. **Rank test under `check_stability=True`** (`Analysis._check_stability`, still the default for every analysis method). Per-DOF zero-stiffness scan first (relative to each row's largest term, so it works in any unit system), then a rank test on the *partitioned* matrix the solver actually inverts: symmetric row-max equilibration → `splu`/`lu_factor` pivot ratio (SVD fallback if scipy is absent) → singular when `min|Uᵢᵢ|/max|Uᵢᵢ| ≤ max(n,100)·eps`, the standard `matrix_rank` tolerance. Inverse iteration names the participating DOFs on the console (`node p2 … global Y direction`), capped at 10 lines with a summary.
2. **Always-on solution validation** (`Analysis._solve_displacements` / `_validate_displacements`), used by `analyze`, `analyze_linear`, `analyze_PDelta` and `analyze_pushover`: every solved vector must be finite and satisfy `‖K₁₁D₁ − P‖∞ ≤ 1e-3·‖P‖∞`. Supported models land at ~1e-10; mechanisms at ~2+. It runs inside the original `try` blocks, so the documented exception types and messages are unchanged.

Calibration margin: supported models (incl. 1e6 rigid links, mile-scale units, 2646-DOF meshes) keep pivot ratios ≥ 2.6e-4; mechanisms ≤ 3.5e-17 (2.25e-14 at n=2646) — ≥26× headroom, and ill-conditioning up to ~1e10 stiffness contrast still solves.

## Verification

- `python reproduce.py` → exit 0, `workflow_completed`; `frame_a` completed and finite on all four paths, `frame_b` `analysis_exception`/`Exception` on all four.
- `devtests/compare_with_baseline.py` (materializes `HEAD` via `git archive` and re-runs everything): **232 analyses compared, 0 supported-structure results changed** (bit-identical), 34 previously-misreported unsupported analyses now rejected.
- `devtests/test_stability.py`: **250 passed** — 22 supported models (frames, trusses with tethered rotations, springs 1e-6…1e12, quad/plate/mat/shear-wall meshes, enforced displacements, tension-only, multi-combo, P-Delta, pushover, modal) vs 7 unsupported ones across both methods × both solvers, closed-form checks, `check_stability=False` contract, no-scipy dense path, plus guards proving no fixture names/numbers entered the library and that the workbench/fixtures are untouched.
- Faster than the snapshot with the check on (n=14406: 9.47 s → 5.13 s), since the old check did an O(n·nodes) Python lookup.
- `source/docs/source/stability.rst` documents both layers.
